paperTitle: O-Level English 1184 Paper 2 Section B — The Uniform
note: AI-authored original narrative for O-Level §B style practice; not from a past examination paper. 出处说明仅作内部记录，不得写进 passage 正文（学生可见）。

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
The uniform came to me in a plastic bag from my cousin Wei Ming, who had outgrown it and who had never, in four years, treated anything gently. The white shirt had gone the colour of weak tea at the collar. There was a shadow on the left pocket where a badge had been unpicked, and a small tear near the hem that somebody had already mended once, badly, in the wrong shade of thread.

Paragraph 2
My mother spread it out on the dining table and looked at it the way she looked at vegetables at the market, turning it over, pressing the seams flat with the side of her hand. 'Good cloth,' she said. 'Still strong.' I said nothing. In three weeks I would walk into a new school in a shirt that had already been somebody's for four years, and I could not think of a single thing about that which was good.

Paragraph 3
She soaked it that night in a basin on the kitchen floor. I heard her at it after I had gone to bed — the slow squeak of cloth against the ridged board, the water changing, the tap running and stopping and running again. In the morning the shirt was on the pole outside the window, and the collar was not white, exactly, but it was no longer the colour of tea.

Paragraph 4
Then she took out the tin. It had once held biscuits and now held everything else: buttons, safety pins, a tape measure gone soft with age, and a bundle of thread wound onto a scrap of card. She measured me twice, standing me by the window where the light was better. She took the shoulders in. She let the sleeves down and pressed the old fold flat with a wet cloth and the iron, over and over, until the line where the hem had been almost disappeared.

Paragraph 5
It took her four evenings. She did it after dinner, after the washing, sitting on the low stool with the shirt across her knees and her head bent so close to the cloth that I wondered how she could see anything at all. I sat at the table with my books open and did not offer to help, and she did not ask, and neither of us said anything about the fact that a new shirt from the shop in the town centre cost eighteen dollars.

Paragraph 6
On the first morning I put it on and it fitted. It fitted better than anything I had ever worn. The shoulders sat where shoulders are supposed to sit and the cuffs stopped exactly at my wrist, and when I turned in front of the mirror I could not find the mend near the hem at all. My mother came and stood behind me and straightened the collar with two fingers, which she did not need to do, and then she went to make the coffee.

Paragraph 7
A boy in my new class asked, that first week, where I got my shirt done, because his always bunched at the back. I heard myself say that my mother had made it, and it was only afterwards, walking home, that I understood I had not said it to cover anything up. There had been nothing in my voice to cover.

Paragraph 8
I kept that shirt until it was truly finished, two years later, and I have never since been able to look at a shop window full of new clothes without thinking of a low stool and a bent head and four evenings of somebody's eyesight. She had not been saving eighteen dollars. She had been making sure that nobody would ever look at me the way I had looked at that plastic bag.

(Glossary: pole: a bamboo drying pole extended from a flat's window, common in older Singapore housing; town centre: the shopping area at the heart of a housing estate.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, who had owned the uniform before the narrator? [1]
Q2. From Paragraph 5, how many evenings did the narrator's mother spend altering the shirt? [1]
Q3. What does the phrase 'the colour of weak tea' in 'The white shirt had gone the colour of weak tea at the collar' (Paragraph 1) suggest about the shirt? [1]
questions.answer: that the collar had yellowed / become stained a pale brown with age and long wear, and was no longer properly white

questions.stem: Q4. What does the word 'shadow' in 'There was a shadow on the left pocket where a badge had been unpicked' (Paragraph 1) suggest? [1]
questions.answer: that the cloth under the old badge had stayed a different, darker shade, leaving a visible mark of what had been removed

questions.stem: Q5. What does the writer suggest about the mother by comparing her examination of the shirt to the way 'she looked at vegetables at the market' (Paragraph 2)? [1]
questions.answer: that she assessed it practically and expertly, judging its quality and what could be made of it rather than reacting to how it looked

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain why the narrator 'said nothing' when his mother called the cloth 'good' (Paragraph 2). [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (he disagreed): he saw only a worn, second-hand shirt and could find nothing good in it at all; MP2 (but he did not argue): he understood that a complaint would be pointless or would sound ungrateful, since the family could not simply buy a new one. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain what the detail about the eighteen-dollar shirt tells the reader, given that 'neither of us said anything' about it. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (money was the real reason): the family could not afford a new shirt, which is why the old one had to be remade; MP2 (it was left unspoken): both mother and son were aware of this and deliberately avoided naming it, out of pride or to spare each other embarrassment. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain why the mother straightened a collar that 'she did not need to' straighten. (Paragraph 6) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (pride in her work): the small unnecessary touch was her way of admiring the result and taking quiet satisfaction in what she had made; MP2 (affection she could not say aloud): it was a gesture of love and care from someone who expressed such things through her hands rather than in words. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q9. What is the effect of the narrator's realisation that there 'had been nothing in my voice to cover'? (Paragraph 7) [2]
questions.answer: it marks the exact point at which his shame disappears: he notices his own tone only after the fact, which shows the change was genuine rather than a decision he made, and the quiet, almost accidental way he discovers it makes the shift in feeling more convincing than any declaration would have been

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of the closing sentence, 'She had not been saving eighteen dollars. She had been making sure that nobody would ever look at me the way I had looked at that plastic bag.'? [2]
questions.answer: the two short parallel sentences reject the obvious explanation and replace it with a deeper one, turning an act that looked like thrift into an act of protection; the return to the plastic bag from the opening closes the story on the narrator's own earlier contempt, so the final judgement falls on him rather than on the shirt

Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's feelings about the second-hand uniform change over the course of the story. For each part of the passage, choose ONE word from the bank that best describes his dominant feeling at that moment. There are some extra words in the bank you do not need to use, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: alarmed / amused / dismayed / grateful / impatient / indifferent / proud / resentful.
